title: Egypt, the Proud River Monster
overview: Ezekiel announces that Egypt's king will be humbled for his pride and for failing Israel, and later adds that Egypt will be handed to Babylon's king.

parts.label: The crocodile of the Nile (vv. 1-6a)
parts.note: Dated to about 587 BC, while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, this pictures Pharaoh (probably Hophra) as a huge crocodile who claims he made the Nile himself. Like a crocodile hooked and dragged onto dry land with fish clinging to its scales, he and everyone who depends on him will be left to die in the open.

parts.label: A reed that splinters (vv. 6b-7)
parts.note: Judah had leaned on Egypt to help it resist Babylon, and an Egyptian army did briefly draw Babylon away from Jerusalem before the siege resumed. Egypt is compared to a Nile reed used as a walking stick that snaps and cuts the hand of whoever leans on it.

parts.label: Ruin and scattering (vv. 8-12)
parts.note: The poetic picture is now spelled out: war will empty Egypt from Migdol in the north to Aswan in the south, and its people will be scattered. History records no forty years of total emptiness, so many read the number as symbolic, echoing Israel's forty years in the wilderness after leaving Egypt.

parts.label: A smaller Egypt returns (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: Egypt will be restored, but to its southern heartland and as a minor kingdom that never again dominates other nations. Israel will then stop trusting Egypt, and Egypt will serve as a reminder of that misplaced trust.

parts.label: Egypt as Babylon's pay (vv. 17-20)
parts.note: This later message, from about 571 BC, is the latest dated one in the book. Babylon's long siege of Tyre wore out its soldiers but brought little plunder, so Egypt's wealth is promised as their wages, which many scholars see as an adjustment to the earlier prophecy about Tyre.

parts.label: A horn for Israel (vv. 21)
parts.note: A horn stands for strength, so this promises that Israel's strength will grow again, and that Ezekiel will be able to speak freely once his words come true. Christians have read the rising horn as pointing ahead to Jesus.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether verses 17 to 20 show a prophecy being revised when events turned out differently at Tyre, or whether the earlier words about Tyre were fulfilled in a way these verses simply clarify.
think: What in your life do you tend to think of as entirely your own making, and how does that view hold up when you look at it closely?
